explanations.answer: The kings and all the people
explanations.explanation: That's the one, baker. The LORD says, "Hear the word of the LORD, O kings of Judah, all people of Judah and Jerusalem who enter through these gates." (Jeremiah 17:20) Kings and regular folks get the very same message at the very same gate. Nobody gets a side door.

Elders and judges are not named here, friend. The LORD calls out "O kings of Judah, all people of Judah and Jerusalem who enter through these gates." (Jeremiah 17:20) So the message goes to the kings and everybody walking through. Nobody in that crowd gets to say the memo wasn't for them.

Priests and prophets don't show up in this call, baker. The LORD says, "Hear the word of the LORD, O kings of Judah, all people of Judah and Jerusalem who enter through these gates." (Jeremiah 17:20) That's the kings plus everyone coming through. It's a message for the whole gate traffic.

Not quite, friend. The LORD says, "stand at the gate of the people… and stand at all the other gates of Jerusalem." (Jeremiah 17:19) So the gate of the people is just the first stop. Jeremiah has a lot of walking ahead of him.

That's right, baker. The LORD says, "Go and stand at the gate of the people, through which the kings of Judah go in and out; and stand at all the other gates of Jerusalem." (Jeremiah 17:19) So it's the gate of the people AND all the others. That's one very tired set of sandals by the end of the day.

Yes, baker. The LORD says, "do not carry a load or bring it through the gates of Jerusalem on the Sabbath day." (Jeremiah 17:21) The warning is about loads coming through those gates. Even a heavy day of hauling had to stop for the Sabbath.

Crowds aren't mentioned, friend. The warning says, "do not carry a load or bring it through the gates of Jerusalem on the Sabbath day." (Jeremiah 17:21) The trouble is a load going through the gates. Standing around is not the issue here.

Gate opening times don't come up, baker. The LORD says, "do not carry a load or bring it through the gates of Jerusalem on the Sabbath day." (Jeremiah 17:21) The command is about carrying a load through. Nothing about sunrise at all.

That's right, friend. The LORD says, "You must not carry a load out of your houses or do any work on the Sabbath day." (Jeremiah 17:22) So the rule reaches right into people's homes. No sneaking a load out the back door either.

Not this time, baker. The LORD says, "You must not carry a load out of your houses or do any work on the Sabbath day." (Jeremiah 17:22) So houses are covered along with the gates. The rule follows people all the way home.

Right on, friend. The LORD says, "but you must keep the Sabbath day holy, just as I commanded your forefathers." (Jeremiah 17:22) No loads and no work, and the day is kept holy. That's the whole point of the day.

The king isn't in this command, baker. The LORD says, "but you must keep the Sabbath day holy, just as I commanded your forefathers." (Jeremiah 17:22) The day is kept holy before the LORD. Even the kings were being told to hear this.

Fasting isn't mentioned here, friend. The LORD says, "but you must keep the Sabbath day holy, just as I commanded your forefathers." (Jeremiah 17:22) The word is holy. A lot of cookie-free grumbling isn't part of it.

Not what the text says, baker. It says, "Yet they would not listen or incline their ear, but they stiffened their necks and would not listen or receive My discipline." (Jeremiah 17:23) So the forefathers did not listen. That's the whole problem the LORD is pointing at.

Yes, friend. The LORD says, "Yet they would not listen or incline their ear, but they stiffened their necks and would not listen or receive My discipline." (Jeremiah 17:23) The forefathers heard the command and would not listen. That's a rough report card.

That's right, baker. The LORD says that if they listen and keep the Sabbath day holy, "then kings and princes will enter through the gates of this city." (Jeremiah 17:25) They ride in with their officials, too. The gates would be busy in the best way.

Not quite, friend. The LORD says that if the people listen and keep the Sabbath holy, "then kings and princes will enter through the gates of this city." (Jeremiah 17:25) They come riding in chariots and on horses. So the promise is a good one.
Yes, baker. The LORD says, "this city will be inhabited forever." (Jeremiah 17:25) That's the promise if the people listen. Forever is a long time to keep the lights on.
That's too short, friend. The LORD says, "this city will be inhabited forever." (Jeremiah 17:25) "For now" sounds like a lease I'd get on a bakery, not His promise. His word is forever.
Close in sound, baker, but not the word. The LORD says, "this city will be inhabited forever." (Jeremiah 17:25) Not once more. Forever, which is a whole lot more than a second helping.

That's it, friend. People come "bringing burnt offerings and sacrifices, grain offerings and frankincense, and thank offerings to the house of the LORD." (Jeremiah 17:26) They arrive from all over with their gifts. That's a full parade of folks coming to worship.

No taxes here, baker. The LORD says people come "bringing burnt offerings and sacrifices, grain offerings and frankincense, and thank offerings to the house of the LORD." (Jeremiah 17:26) These are offerings for worship. Nobody's filling out forms at the door.

Tools aren't on the list, friend. The LORD says people come "bringing burnt offerings and sacrifices, grain offerings and frankincense, and thank offerings to the house of the LORD." (Jeremiah 17:26) They bring offerings to the house of the LORD. Leave the hammers at home.

You got it, baker. The LORD says He will "kindle an unquenchable fire in its gates to consume the citadels of Jerusalem." (Jeremiah 17:27) The fire starts at the gates and the citadels are what it consumes. It's a heavy warning, and the LORD says it plainly.

Benjamin shows up in the good news, friend. People come from "the land of Benjamin" bringing offerings. (Jeremiah 17:26) But the fire in verse 27 is about Jerusalem, where it consumes "the citadels of Jerusalem." (Jeremiah 17:27) It's a heavy part of the passage.

The Negev is part of the good news, baker. People come from "the hill country, and the Negev" bringing offerings. (Jeremiah 17:26) The fire, though, is set to "consume the citadels of Jerusalem." (Jeremiah 17:27) It's a heavy warning, so let's take it seriously.
